Additional Notes: I wrote this article because I want more involvement from the MCF. The MCF looks like joke in some perspective but this article would give it maybe more attention and mystery. I already made a draft and if you look to give a feedback or greenlight just reply. I made I few adjustments to my article. Just ask for the sandbox. Feel free to criticize

item.title: Seeking Greenlight - Man in the Mirror
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Elevator Pitch: The SCP refers to a hypothetical anomaly. A new "Foundation," which operates extraordinarily similarly to ours, almost the exact same but for a few differences, which has been clearly operating for years upon years, has suddenly come to our knowledge. Surely, the only way they've been existing for so long without us knowing is if they were using an anomaly to hide themselves… right? Surely, no one matches the Foundation in their ability to hide themselves from the rest of the world…

Right?

Central Narrative: The narrative is going to follow the first encounter between our SCP Foundation, and the PCS Foundation (Process, Condemn, Shield), and then followed up by a MTF exploration of a PCS facility in hunting for the SCP, then recounting an exact replica of the events that occurred at the PCS facility, except it's an interview recounting the exact same events occurring at a SCP facility. By the end, no actual SCP is recovered, or even hinted at existing, hopefully leaving the reader asking if it's possible that just maybe two foundations were so good at hiding that up until now, they hid from each other.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: I know theoretical/non-existent SCPs have been done before, but I'm hoping the description here is enough of a hook to keep things going.

Additional Notes: I know I'm not the greatest at summarizations. It may need some.. work. I'd be happy to clarify anything if the need should be there. Additionally, I sort of jumped the gun and wrote up an unfinished draft. If anyone would like, I'd be happy to let you read it, although it needs some heavy revising.

item.title: Re: A Photo Book of Murderers
item.content:encoded:
1) There are plenty of stories, between trepanning, lobotomy, and the various eugenics tactics, so there should be plenty of fun in that regard. There should be plenty of additional stories in a universe where people sacrifice to eldritch horrors.

2) The basic problem is that you delve too much into the hook and not enough into the photobooks themselves. There are no mechanics on how it works, how a killer is determined for the person in question, not even if it is permanent or temporary. You have an interesting idea, but the item itself just isn't described to any degree. Heck, there's not even a lot of history given on it, and what little history there is doesn't really set it up.

3) In that regard, you have way too much hook. In fact, most of the central narrative is nothing but hook. Summarize it and add it to the hook section, and then go back and build your central narrative. You've got a great hook; you just need some actual details.

item.title: Re: TICKY TAFFY TOWN (Seeking Greenlight)
item.content:encoded:
This is actually a fun idea, as weird as I know that sounds. While there are a number of Kid-TV SCP's, this is just different enough from them that it could work.

1) You need to flesh it out a bit. There's just nothing really here; it's just a skeleton. To whom or what the sacrifice is to needs to be better defined. There is also an issue in how so many kids are killed on a regular basis without anyone finding out; even if you used nothing but runaways and orphans the murder toll would create curiosity at some point.

2) The UIU doesn't hand cases off to The Foundation without a good reason. Why did they do that this time?

It's an excellent start, it just needs some fleshing out.

item.title: Re: An atavistic humanoid + a mysterious organization
item.content:encoded:
1) You need to seriously cut down the number of words; Elevator Pitch, Central Narrative, Hook, and Additional Notes need to be about 400 words. You can eliminate the additional notes: You don't need names and you may want to drop the idea for an organization (more on that below). That's your first 43 words.

2) You may want to look into the current GOI to find a group that works for you. The obvious suggestions are Herman Fuller's Circus of the Disquieting (using a program to create circus freaks), Prometheus Labs (one group could be interested in developing prehistoric individuals to test some theories), or even a Sarkic Cult. This will save you a lot of work and stress.

3) You need to define what the humanoid can do better. Telepathy and mental compulsion are different abilities; if it can read minds that works well with the story. A telepathic caveman is a great idea, by the way.

4) Other than that, it looks like you are looking more at a Tale than an actual article. If done as an article, including the information about the spy and its resolution needs to be included as a very clinical addendum, with just the facts. So keep that in mind if you end up writing this up.

5) Also, it's "trait".

item.title: Re: SCP Idea: Conehead
item.content:encoded:
1) Keep in mind that you need about two weeks between posts.

2) In terms of what it is and what it can do, this is an interesting idea. However, it doesn't appear to have a reason for being; it just is. This is sort of why you need to look at the hook; it has to have something that draws in the crowd.

There are two options: Either fit it into the ecology of the universe as a whole give it some sort of symbolic purpose. It's can be a carnivore or a hunter of some sort that is looking for something. It doesn't need to be looking for something to eat; it could be looking for sources of magic or the exotic particles it needs to live. They could even be pets of someone that for whatever reason (the master let them go, they died, or they could have been captured) have their freedom.

Conversely, they could serve as a living symbol of something. As they can't be looked at or even see themselves without confusing themselves, something linked to vanity would be natural. It's also incomplete; that people don't like the incomplete or things that are missing something could fit into it as well.

Like I said: It's a great idea. We're just lacking a reason to care about it that is missing.

item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Genre: Comedy

Page Layout: An initial standard page going over the published editions of the book, and a log of incomplete and poorly copied extracts of the text without magic supposedly due to low quality. Followed by an up-to-date article documenting a edited copy of the tome, with a log of the different corrections made by a disenfranchised undergraduate of the establishment that require the book. Containment procedures allow for the book to be borrowed by approved request.

Elevator Pitch: A secondhand university thaumaturgy textbook which is defunct and a scam, corrected by a angry ex-student (of the institution using it as required reading) to make it functional.

+ Show whatever
- Hide whatever

Central Narrative: The book is drawn to the foundation's attention when it is incredulously found via web-crawlers on online book. It is quickly scrubbed from the website due to Foundation concerns about secrecy. A team of researchers are tasked with tracking down copies of the book but all that can be found are monochrome, poorly reproduced photocopies which are useless assisting thaumaturgical practices.

They receive a package from a disgruntled student of a only to discover it is a textbook for a specific professor who charges $25,000 USD (or relative small fortune) or "a year's servitude to dark forces" for it. The book is covered in angry notes expressing frustration in the inaccuracies of it such as " What am I supposed to use?? Pig's blood or wolf?" and "There's no godsdamn way that is an acceptable salt circle", as well as several corrections in order to make the rituals and magic work as intended. The Foundation reclassifies the published versions as non-anomalous and classifies the only anomalous version to be the corrected one.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: The thaumaturgy methods and descriptions in an academic way and the premise that not even magic prevents you from being screwed over by the educational system.

Additional Notes: Would appreciate idea on how the actual corrected book is anomalous and not just containing data that can be used to create anomalies, and any areas of thaumaturgy on the SCP universe I should try and include in the photocopy example extracts?

So it looks like this article is heading into the deletion range. I know that can often feel baffling or upsetting for a first time writer (trust me, you get used to it!), so please take this feedback as advice on your next SCP! If feedback seems harsh, it’s only because I hate when authors keep making the same mistakes until they give up on the wiki. Keep trying, you’ll get there!

Here are a few pitfalls you fell into:

SCP’s are written in clinical, precise language. This piece reads like prose, when a SCP should read like a formal scientific document. I strongly recommend reading the Clinical Tone Guide. Here are a few examples.

“a small table all the way in the back of the chamber”

“All the way in the back” is a very casual way of describing something. “Small” is imprecise.

“Whatever the wearer believes becomes real, and that's anything. Even accidentally.”

Sentence fragments used for emphasis can work in traditional prose, but are out of place in formal scientific writing.

“SCP-5129 seems to be rather “squared”, as if it was what could only be described as “8-bit”.”

“Seems to be” isn’t a great way to describe a SCP. The fictional reader isn’t interested in what it seems to be, they want to know what it is and what it looks like. If there’s a difference between what it is and what it looks like, that should be clear. Using “rather” is imprecise as well.

Beyond the writing style, the content of the SCP has some more fundamental issues. For one, your containment procedures are pretty overblown. From what I can tell, the glasses are only dangerous if somebody touches them. That makes them about as dangerous as a sample of smallpox or a piece of uranium, which is to say, Safe. Euclid is for objects that are unpredictable and need active containment, whereas this thing is fine as long as you don’t poke it. Lock it in a very secure box and don’t let anybody touch it. If you want to be extremely careful, maybe embed it in a block of plastic first. Bam, done.

There’s no narrative arc or story to this piece. Another commenter addressed this above, but basically, you’ve given us this interesting object that can cause all sorts of mayhem and a few lines of mystery about where it came from, but you haven’t gone anywhere with either premise. It’s all setup, with no conclusion.

Mystery and ambiguity is good, but it should be the sort of thing that leaves the reader asking questions once the story is complete. This piece asks the reader to construct a story purely in their head, but is too vague and open-ended to give us the momentum to get there. The payoff to a story can be a sense of horror or mystery, but it still has to be a payoff.

Hope at least some of this helps. I look forward to reading your next article! The wiki has a pretty high attrition rate, so don’t be too discouraged if it takes a while to get one to stick.

It looks like you're trying to set up a mystery in your central narrative (how did this man get all these quarters?) but the answer to the mystery isn't particularly interesting (an anomaly that makes quarters out of nothing).

Compare your mystery to something like SCP-5005 (spoilers ahead BTW). One of the mysteries 5005 sets up is "where did this giant magic lamp come from?" and the answer is "it's the lure of a massive anglerfish". Once you know the answer, the complete situation "this town exists in a sea of nothingness because of the light of a giant dead anglerfish's lure" is a lot more interesting than "this guy has a lot of quarters because he has an SCP that makes quarters".

The simplest solution would be changing your anomaly so that there's some deeper implication to making all those quarters. Say, for example, that the anomaly is a machine that grinds cute baby animals into a pulp and then turns them into quarters. Now, your complete situation isn't just "this guy has a lot of quarters because he has an SCP that makes quarters"— it's "this guy has a lot of quarters because he was willing to grind up tons of cute baby animals for money."

item.title: Re: Almost Ideal

These would be a pretty clear-cut Safe object- lock them in a box and never open it again, nothing bad will happen.

I like to point to SCP-2948 as the ultimate "dangerous safe" object- it's a literal nuclear bomb with unlimited yield… but it's safe because they've disabled the countdown timer and put it in a very sturdy box.
